# Allelic Typing (cgMLST) {#sec-tech-typing}

Typing is the central pipeline: it turns a whole-genome assembly into an allele
profile in the database. This chapter follows one assembly through the code — the
view module that accepts it, the shell script that drives the external toolchain,
how the results are parsed back, the classical 7-gene ST resolved alongside, and
the provenance and hashing recorded so a call can be traced.

## The typing view module {#sec-tech-typing-ui}

`app/view/typing.R` accepts one or more assembly FASTA files (`.fasta`, `.fa` or
`.fna`), shows live progress as each is typed, and reports per-isolate outcomes.
Because typing is long-running and writes the same `.db` the rest of the app
reads, it runs in a **separate process** and coordinates through the busy-timeout
armed on every connection (@sec-db-connect) and the revision bus, which it bumps
(`isolates`, `amr`) when new isolates land so every reader refreshes
(@sec-arch-signals).

## The external toolchain {#sec-tech-typing-toolchain}

All computationally intensive work happens in the Conda environment
(@sec-arch-conda), reached through `app/logic/pymlst.R`. The conda executable is
resolved carefully (preferring `CONDA_EXE` over any env-local `conda`,
`conda_exe()`), and the run is assembled and launched by:

```{.r filename="app/logic/pymlst.R"}
#' Execute Synchronous Genome Typing Pipeline
type_genomes <- function(...) { ... }
#' Launch Background Typing Process
start_typing <- function(...) { ... }
```

The actual command sequence lives in the shell script `app/logic/loop-pymlst.sh`,
which `start_typing()` launches as a background process and whose log
`app/view/typing.R` tails for progress. `typing_args()` builds the arguments.

### The order of operations {#sec-tech-typing-order}

The three tool invocations are **sequential steps over the same assembly**, not a
fan-out: `wgMLST add` does not trigger `claMLST search`, and neither triggers the
AMR screen. `process_genome()` in `loop-pymlst.sh` runs them one after another
for each file in turn, and steps 2 and 3 are best-effort — each is skipped
silently if its prerequisites were not supplied, without affecting the cgMLST
call:

```{.bash filename="app/logic/loop-pymlst.sh"}
# --- Step 1: cgMLST Allele Calling ---
"$CONDA" run -n "$env" wgMLST add "$db" "$file" --strain "$strain_name" ...

# --- Step 2: Classical MLST (Best-Effort) ---
if [[ -n "$CLA_DB" && -f "$CLA_DB" ]]; then
    cla_out=$("$CONDA" run -n "$env" claMLST search -i "$id" -c "$cov" "$CLA_DB" "$file" ...)
fi

# --- Step 3: AMR Screening (Best-Effort via abritamr / AMRFinderPlus) ---
if [[ -n "$AMR_OUT" && -n "$AMR_ENV" ]]; then
    timeout -k 30 1200 "$CONDA" run --no-capture-output -n "$AMR_ENV" \
        abritamr run -c "$file" -px "$amr_prefix" ...
fi
```

The classical reference database is built **once before the loop**, not per
genome: R resolves the scheme (@sec-tech-typing-classical), writes a spec file,
and the script downloads exactly the profile table and allele files that spec
names and runs `claMLST create`.

Only step 1 writes to the loaded `.db` directly, from inside the pyMLST process.
Steps 2 and 3 write to the run log and to a temporary output directory; R parses
those and performs the corresponding database writes itself once the isolate is
finished.


## Reading the run: results and calls {#sec-tech-typing-results}

pyMLST's output and logs are parsed into structured tables by `pymlst.R`. The
cgMLST outcome per strain is summarised (`cg_outcome()`), and the log is turned
into a per-isolate table (`parse_typing_log()`) recording loci found, alleles
added, partial and filled genes, identity/coverage and completeness. These feed
both the on-screen results and the provenance row
(@sec-tech-typing-provenance).

Helper queries expose the database's typing state to the UI: `existing_strains()`
(what is already typed, so duplicates can be flagged), `scheme_size()` (total
loci), `strain_gene_counts()` (called loci per isolate), and `hashes_pending()`
(whether any typed sequence still lacks a hash — used to decide whether a reload
needs to backfill, @sec-arch-nav).

## Classical MLST alongside cgMLST {#sec-tech-typing-classical}

Resolving *which* 7-gene scheme to use is non-trivial, and
`app/logic/mlst_repo.R` exists to do it deterministically:

```{.r filename="app/logic/mlst_repo.R"}
# pyMLST's own `claMLST import` searches ... by fuzzy substring match and refuses
# to guess whenever more than one hit comes back, which silently loses the ST for
# species whose repository holds several schemes (Enterococcus faecium) and can
# just as silently settle on the wrong genus. This module resolves the database
# and the scheme itself - genus always enforced, never more than one candidate
# accepted - and hands the exact download URLs to loop-pymlst.sh ...
```

`resolve_mlst_scheme()` queries the PubMLST and Institut Pasteur REST APIs,
enforcing the genus and accepting exactly one scheme candidate; `claMLST create`
then builds the reference locally from the URLs it names. Results are persisted
by `store_clamlst_results()` into `classical_mlst` in one transaction.

::: {.callout-important title="pyMLST mangles species names — so the resolver reproduces the damage"}
`mlst_repo.R` contains `mangle_species()`, which deliberately *reproduces*
pyMLST's letter-dropping so a database's stored (possibly mangled) species can
still be matched, and `canonical_species()`, which repairs it. The ST call itself
is resolved by `clamlst_status()`, `parse_allele_spec()`, `st_from_profile()` and
`resolve_clamlst_call()` — the search's own call is authoritative whenever it
settled on a single ST, with a profile-table fallback for edge cases such as the
*pstS* deletion in *Enterococcus faecium*.
:::

## Assembly identity and duplicate detection {#sec-tech-typing-hashing}

Every assembly is fingerprinted so silent duplicates can be caught.
`genome_hash.R` computes a GA4GH-style content digest and records it against the
isolate:

```{.r filename="app/logic/genome_hash.R"}
#' Normalizes sequence contigs, computes refget digests per contig, and hashes
#' [them into a single genome digest].
genome_digest <- function(path) { ... }   # sha512t24u, RFC 4648 §5 base64url
store_genome_hash <- function(db_path, strain, genome_file, digest = NULL) { ... }
```

Before typing, `check_genomes()` / `classify_genome()` compare the incoming
assembly's digest and name against what is recorded and classify each as **new**,
an **identical re-type** (same digest, same name), or a **duplicate** (same
content, different name — or a name clash pyMLST would reject as
`StrainAlreadyPresent`, surfaced as "Duplicate").

::: {.callout-important title="The digest flags, it never blocks"}
The genome digest is a *one-way indicator*. A match proves two runs consumed the
byte-identical assembly; a mismatch proves nothing (re-assembling the same reads
with a different assembler yields a different digest). It is therefore used to
*flag* likely duplicates, never as a hard constraint that could incorrectly block
a legitimate re-analysis. Do not promote it to a uniqueness constraint.
:::

## Provenance: how each isolate was typed {#sec-tech-typing-provenance}

As the run proceeds, `app/logic/provenance.R` writes one wide row per isolate to
`typing_provenance` — the single place a finished isolate can be traced back to
the software and reference data that produced it:

```{.r filename="app/logic/provenance.R"}
#' Called once per isolate for every step that reports in, so the row grows as
#' the run goes.
store_provenance <- function(db_path, isolate, fields) { ... }
```

It records the assembly digest, the cgMLST scheme/version/seed genome and
thresholds, the classical scheme, the AMR run, and the exact tool versions
(`pymlst`, `blat`, `mafft`, AMRFinderPlus) — parsed from the logs by
`parse_clamlst_meta()`, `parse_tool_meta()` and `parse_amr_meta()`. The scheme
columns are denormalized on purpose: they snapshot what was true at typing time,
so a later scheme refresh cannot rewrite a call's history (@sec-database).

## Chapter summary

- `typing.R` types in a separate process, coordinating through the busy timeout
  and the revision bus.
- `loop-pymlst.sh` runs three **sequential** steps per assembly — `wgMLST add`,
  then `claMLST search`, then `abritamr run`; the classical reference is built
  once before the loop.
- Only step 1 writes the `.db` from inside pyMLST; R parses the log and performs
  the classical/AMR/hash/provenance writes itself.
- `mlst_repo.R` resolves the classical scheme deterministically (genus enforced,
  one candidate), robust to pyMLST's species-name mangling.
- Every assembly is content-hashed for duplicate detection; every isolate gets a
  full `typing_provenance` row.

AMR screening is step 3 of the same run — that is @sec-tech-amr.
